blocks.text: And Arrian in the Alexander: Χάλυβες πρῶτοι ἀνθρώπων αἰτίαν ἔχουσι χαλκεύσασθαι σίδηρον [Chalybes prōtoi anthrōpōn aitian echousi chalkeusasthai sidēron]; the Chalybes are charged with having been the first to forge iron. And Ammianus, book 22: the Chalybes, by whom iron was first dug out and worked. Yet others attribute the same invention to the Cyclopes. Pliny, book 7, chapter 56: Some think that the Chalybes, others that the Cyclopes [II, 442] first showed the craft of working bronze. However that may be, from the frequent digging of metals the land of the Chalybes could be called Chaldia, and its inhabitants Chaldi, Chaldii and Chaldaei. For that the ancients wrote it in all these ways is attested by Eustathius in his Notes on Dionysius Periegetes, page 101 b. And these names clearly allude to the verb חלד chalad, which, when said of the earth, means to dig, as was proved at length above ^{c)}. Now who does not see that the name חולד choled can fittingly be referred to the same root, for the mole, which seems born and designed for this very purpose: to undermine and dig beneath the earth with unceasing labour? That is why no one defines the mole without making this part of the definition. Thus in Hesychius, under the words Λὼτ [Lōt] and Σκάλοψ [Skalops], we read that it is μῦς τυφλὸς ὁ τὴν γῆν τρυπῶν [mys typhlos ho tēn gēn trypōn], a blind mouse that bores through the earth; and ζῶον γεώρυχον τυφλὸν [zōon geōrychon typhlon], a blind animal that digs the earth. Epiphanius, on the Adamites, right at the beginning: Ἀσπάλακα καλοῦσί τι ζῶον ἐν τῇ γῇ κάτω ἐμφωλεῦον, τετράπουν, ὅπερ ὀρύττει τὴν γῆν [Aspalaka kalousi ti zōon en tē gē katō emphōleuon, tetrapoun, hoper oryttei tēn gēn], etc. They call mole a certain four-footed animal that has its lairs in the depths of the earth, which it digs out, etc. In Jerome on Isaiah, chapter 2: It is an animal without eyes, which is always digging the earth and throwing up the soil. In R. Solomon on the same passage: חפרפרות מיני שרצים שחופרין הארץ שקורין טלפא בלעז, Chaphorpheroth are kinds of creeping things that dig the earth, and in the vernacular are called talpae [moles]. And in Moed Katan fol. 6 b: בריה שאין לה עיניים חופרת בקרקע It is a creature that lacks eyes and digs in the earth. Accordingly, naturalists note that its very sharp snout serves this purpose. And the forward part of its forelegs has this peculiarity, that it consists of paired and very short bones, which are inserted directly into the humerus, so that they may dig more powerfully. For the same reason the forefeet and toes point not downward but sideways; and they have a quite broad palm and very strong claws, far larger in proportion to the size of the body than in other animals. Hence they dig the earth so easily and so swiftly as almost to pass belief, as we experience daily to the damage of our property. Therefore the other name for moles, חפרפרות, Es. II, 20., is also taken from digging. For, like חלד chalad, חפר chaphar also means to dig, as everyone knows. Hence the reduplicated חפרפרות intensifies the meaning, so that the name designates an animal wholly given over to digging the earth. But the Greek σπάλαξ [spalax] or ἀσπάλαξ [aspalax] must also be referred to the same idea; its true origin has so far escaped the learned. For those who derive it παρὰ τὸ σπᾶν [para to span], that is, from drawing, talk nonsense. Rather, σπάλαξ [spalax] was formed by metathesis from σκάλοψ [skalops], which was the old word for the mole among the Athenians, as we know from Nicocles: Σκάλοψ, ὁ σπάλαξ λέγεται παρὰ [col. 1027] Ἀττικοῖς, ὡς λέγει Νικοκλῆς [Skalops, ho spalax legetai para Attikois, hōs legei Nikoklēs]. So the Etymologicum. And Aristotle confirms it in the Acharnians, where he has σκάλοπας [skalopas] for moles. On this passage the Scholiast: Σκάλοπας] μύας τινὰς, οὓς φαμεν σπάλακας [Skalopas] myas tinas, hous phamen spalakas]. It is called σκάλοψ [skalops], however, not [II, 443] as if κεκαλυμμένους ἔχων τοὺς ὦπας [kekalymmenous echōn tous ōpas], as the Etymologicum idly claims, but ἀπὸ τοῦ σκάλλειν, ἢ σκαλεύειν [apo tou skallein, ē skaleuein], from digging; and by the compound word σκαλόπεζα [skalopeza], as if having digging feet, as in the Poet ἀργυρόπεζα Θέτις [argyropeza Thetis], silver-footed Thetis. Hesychius: Σκάλοψ· σκαλόπεζα, ἀσπάλαξ [Skalops; skalopeza, aspalax]. So it should be read, not σκαλόπετα [skalopeta], as our editions have it. Again, from σκάλοψ [skalops], mole, comes σκαλοπιὰ [skalopia] for a mole's lair, or a heap of earth thrown up by moles. And it must certainly be taken so in these words of Theophrastus, History, book 7, chapter 11, on the roots of the phasganon (or gladiolus): Πολλὰς δὲ εὑρίσκουσι παρὰ ταῖς σκαλοπιαῖς· χαίρει γὰρ, καὶ συλλέγεται τὸ ζῶον [Pollas de heuriskousi para tais skalopiais; chairei gar, kai syllegetai to zōon]. They find many near the scalopiae, or mole-holes; for this animal seeks them and gathers them. Very badly, then, do the translators render it: They find a great many scolopendras near it. Nor is it true, as others hold, that τὴν σκαλοπιὰν [tēn skalopian] is the same as τὴν σκάλοπα [tēn skalopa]. As if someone held that τὴν μυρμηκιὰν [tēn myrmēkian], the ants' nest, were the same as τὴν μύρμηκα [tēn myrmēka], the ant. What I had nearly omitted: in a certain part of France too the mole is called foyon, as fovir is French for to dig, as the late Cappel (ὁ μακαρίτης [ho makaritēs]) observes in the Critica Sacra, page 382. And Gesner, under Talpa, page 932, records several German names for the mole ^{d)} that belong to the same idea. Thus it is common to the Hebrews, the Greeks, the Germans and some of the French to name the mole from digging.
